basics.name: Boxes.py (Florian Festi's open-source laser-cut box and parts generator)
basics.url: https://boxes.hackerspace-bamberg.de/ (online generator, hosted by Hackerspace Bamberg; also mirrored at https://www.festi.info/boxes.py/). Source: https://github.com/florianfesti/boxes (read via raw.githubusercontent.com). Docs: https://florianfesti.github.io/boxes/html/index.html
basics.resource_type: CAD library (Python library plus a web generator and Inkscape plug-in); also usable as an interactive tool
basics.license: Software is GPL v3+ (README and LICENSE.txt). The FAQ says the drawings you generate are NOT covered by the GPL, so you may cut and sell the objects; the author asks people not to resell unmodified generated files. Linking is fine; reusing its code means keeping it GPL
basics.language: English (docs and code); the web generator interface is also translated into German, Spanish, French, Brazilian Portuguese and Simplified Chinese
basics.year: Started around 2013 (edges.py header reads 'Copyright (C) 2013-2016 Florian Festi'); Hackaday.io project page created 30 March 2016; Hackaday Prize entry in 2017 (Hackaday article, 10 March 2021). Latest docs build 'Last updated on Sep 23, 2026'
basics.access_barrier: none for the web generator (runs in the browser, no login); desktop install (Python 3, plus pstoedit for DXF/G-code/PDF) only if you want to run it locally or write your own generators
basics.image_license: Gallery photos (about 172 sample JPGs under static/samples in the repo) and generated previews appear to fall under the repo's GPL v3 licence, as no separate image licence was found [uncertain]
basics.authority_level: community or unvetted (a long-running open-source maker project led by one developer, Florian Festi, with many contributors; not peer-reviewed, but widely used and tested by makers)

coverage.covers: Laser-cut sheet joints and the parts built from them. The core 'edge' types (about 40 edge classes in edges.py) are: finger joints (box joints) for 90-degree corners, with four finger styles (rectangular, springs, barbs, snap); finger-hole edges for T-joints and inner walls; flat dovetail joints for joining pieces in the same plane (JointPanel makes panels larger than the laser bed); flex cuts (kerf bending) for rounded corners and living hinges; pin hinges and hinge pins; chest hinges; cabinet hinges (knuckle hinges with separate eyes); slide-on lids with locking springs; click-on lids (bent-hook snap connectors); stackable edges with feet; grooved edges; gripping edges; mounting edges with keyhole (pear-shaped) screw holes; handle edges; rack (gear rack) edges; bed bolts (captive nut and bolt slots) in finger joints. On top of these sit 182 ready-made generators in 8 groups, including mechanical parts: spur gears, a multi-stage gearbox, planetary gears (one generator marked unstable), timing belt pulleys, a linkage test model, a servo robot arm, NEMA stepper motor mounts, serrated knobs, a bayonet (twist-lock) box, latched service hatches, rolling shutter doors made of flex, sliding lids and drawers, a laser-cutter clamp and holdfast, and test pieces for kerf (burn) and flex settings
coverage.organisation: The web generator groups its 182 generators by what you are making: Boxes, Boxes with flex, Trays and drawer inserts, Shelves, Wall-mounted, Hole patterns, Parts and samples, Misc, and Unstable, with a photo gallery. Joint types are not browsable by name in the web UI; they appear as folded 'edge settings' inside each generator and on the AllEdges demo generator. The API docs list edges by a one-letter code (f/F finger joint, d/D dovetail, X flex, i/j/k hinge, c/C click, R rack...). Easy to use if you know the object you want (a box with a hinged lid), less so if you are looking for a joint type
coverage.scope_match: medium: it is a working catalogue of clever flat-pack joints and moving parts for laser cutting (snap and barbed finger joints, living hinges, printed-in-sheet pin and cabinet hinges, bayonet twist-lock, click-on lids, slide-on lids with spring catches, gear trains, planetary gears, belt pulleys, rack and pinion), but laser cutting is a later, lower-priority making method for the project, and most generators are whole boxes and shelves rather than connection types
coverage.taxonomy_used: Two levels: (1) by object, 8 top-level generator groups plus 'Unstable' (Boxes, Boxes with flex, Trays and drawer inserts, Shelves, Wall-mounted, Hole patterns, Parts and samples, Misc); (2) by edge type, a flat list of about 40 edge classes in the API (straight, finger joint, finger holes, dovetail, flex, hinge, chest hinge, cabinet hinge, slide-on lid, click connector, stackable, grooved, gripping, mounting, handle, rack, rounded triangle), each with a Settings class
coverage.example_types: finger joint (box joint), including 'springs', 'barbs' and 'snap' finger styles; finger-hole T-joint (mortise-and-tab); flat dovetail joint (jigsaw-style panel joint); flex cut living hinge (kerf-bent lattice hinge); laser-cut pin hinge (knuckle hinge with separate pin); chest hinge; cabinet hinge (multi-eye knuckle hinge with a bored pin); slide-on lid with locking springs (sliding lid with detent catch); click-on lid (cantilever snap hook); bayonet lid (twist-lock box of stacked rings); spring-latched service hatch (press-and-slide latch); rolling shutter (tambour door made from flex cuts); stackable edges with feet (nesting/stacking interlock); keyhole mounting slots (pear-shaped screw holes); captive-nut bed bolts in finger joints (T-slot nut and bolt); spur gears; multi-stage gearbox; planetary (epicyclic) gear set; timing belt pulley; rack and pinion edge; linkage test kit (four-bar linkage)
coverage.making_methods: Laser cutting of sheet material (plywood, MDF, acrylic, cardboard, paper); the generated SVG/DXF also works for CNC routing and knife/vinyl cutters. Not aimed at 3D printing
coverage.item_count: 182 generators in the docs list (September 2026); about 40 edge classes in boxes/edges.py; about 172 sample photos in the gallery
coverage.special_behaviours_covered: Compliant: yes, flex cuts (living hinges, rolling shutters, FlexTest samples) and spring/barb/snap finger styles. Indexing/detent and snap-in: partly, via slide-on lid 'locking springs' and click-on lid hooks. Self-locking / twist-lock: yes, the BayonetBox (lugs that lock when twisted). Hand-release only: yes, the SideDoorHousing service hatches use laser-cut spring latches that lock by themselves when closed and open only when pressed in and slid aside (generator source notes); SideHingeBox also has a latch. Gear trains/gearboxes: yes, spur gears, a multi-stage GearBox, Planetary gear sets (Planetary2 'balanced force difference planetary gear' marked not yet working), rack and pinion, timing belt pulleys. Powered connectors: only mounts for motors (NEMA stepper mounts, servo robot arm segments); no electromagnets or solenoid latches. Torque-limiting, one-way/ratchet, over-centre: none found. Print-in-place: not applicable (laser-cut). Adhesives: none, apart from the manual's note that brittle acrylic should be cut undersized to leave a gap for glue while plywood can be press-fitted without glue
coverage.entry_structure: Each generator page has: name, one-line description, a parameter form (sizes in mm, material thickness, burn/kerf correction, edge settings for every joint type used, output format), a live preview of the cut sheet, a gallery photo, and Generate/Download/Save-to-URL/QR-code buttons. The API docs give each edge type's class, settings with default values (mostly as multiples of material thickness) and a short explanation
coverage.audience_level: hobbyist (makerspace laser-cutter users); the Python API is aimed at programmers who want to write their own generators

usefulness.beginner_friendliness: medium: the web form lets a beginner get a working box by entering size, material thickness and kerf, and the FAQ tells beginners to leave edge settings folded. But joint settings are named in code jargon ('burn', 'surroundingspaces', 'edge_width', one-letter edge codes), there is no explanation of when to choose which joint, and the manual admits the burn setting is 'counter intuitive'
usefulness.has_images: yes: a photo gallery of about 172 real, cut-and-assembled sample objects (good quality, maker photos), plus an SVG preview of the cutting plan for every generator; no labelled diagrams explaining how each joint works
usefulness.has_animations: no animations or videos on the pages opened; the SVG preview updates when you change parameters (interactive, but static 2D)
usefulness.gaps: No per-joint explanations or diagrams (joints are only visible inside finished boxes); no guidance on strength, which joint to choose, or glue vs press fit beyond the kerf notes; nothing for 3D printing; only laser-cut sheet geometry; no special behaviours such as ratchets, torque limiting or over-centre latches; gears and planetary parts are basic and one planetary generator is marked unstable; English-only documentation
usefulness.good_for_entry_links: yes: every generator has a stable per-item URL on the web generator, e.g. https://boxes.hackerspace-bamberg.de/BayonetBox?language=en (twist-lock box) and https://boxes.hackerspace-bamberg.de/AllEdges?language=en (all edge types, including finger styles). Parameters can be saved into the URL, so an entry can link to a pre-set example
usefulness.reusable_data: structured: the whole library is a GPL v3 Python repo (boxes/edges.py for joint geometry, boxes/generators/ for 182 generators, boxes/gears.py and boxes/pulley.py), with Sphinx API docs listing every edge and its default settings. The list of generators and edge types can be reused (facts are not copyrightable); copying code or images means following GPL v3
usefulness.maintained: Yes, actively maintained: the docs were rebuilt on 23 September 2026 (Sphinx 9.1.0) and the online generator was live on 25 September 2026. The Hackaday.io project page was 'last updated a year ago', so news goes to GitHub rather than Hackaday
usefulness.ideas_to_borrow: (1) Express every design rule as a multiple of material thickness (finger width 2t, hinge axle 2t, dovetail depth 1.5t) so one rule scales to any sheet; the same trick could scale 3D-printed joint rules to wall thickness or nozzle size. (2) A kerf/clearance test piece (BurnTest, FlexTest) linked from each joint entry, so makers can tune fit before printing the real part. (3) An 'all edges' demo page that shows every joint side by side. (4) 'Save to URL' links that open a generator with the exact settings used in an entry's example. (5) Colour conventions in output files (black outer cut, blue inner cut, red help lines, green engraving). (6) Grouping generators by the object the maker is building as a second way into the catalogue
usefulness.design_rules_given: Yes, for laser-cut joints: finger joint defaults are finger 2t, space 2t, play 0 (t = material thickness); dovetail angle 50 degrees, size 3t, depth 1.5t; flex cut connection 1t, distance 0.5t, width 5t, stretch 1.05; hinge axle 2t, hinge strength 1t; cabinet hinge bore 3.2 mm, eye radius 1.5t, play 0.05t; click-on hooks bend out 5 degrees, depth 3t; gear rack module 3 mm, 20 degree pressure angle. The manual gives kerf tuning in 0.01-0.005 mm steps and says tabs of 0.2-0.3 mm in plywood still let parts be pushed out by hand; snap fingers are only drawn for fingers 1.9t wide or more
usefulness.generator_or_parametric: Yes, fully parametric: 182 web generators and a Python API (turtle-graphics style edge drawing) to write new ones; also runs as an Inkscape extension and from the command line
usefulness.file_formats: SVG and PostScript natively; with pstoedit also DXF, G-code, PDF, PLT (HPGL); LightBurn (lbrn2) and an SVG variant for Ponoko
usefulness.terminology_value: low to medium: uses common maker names (finger joint, dovetail, living hinge, flex, chest hinge, cabinet hinge, bayonet, burn = kerf) but coins its own class names and one-letter codes, and does not give aliases or translations of joint names
usefulness.decision_support: No selector, flow chart or comparison table. Choice is by browsing object groups and the photo gallery, then tuning parameters in a form; the only 'decision' help is the FAQ on fit (thickness, burn) and test-piece generators
usefulness.derived_from_or_overlaps: Original code by Florian Festi and contributors; boxes/gears.py is adapted from the Inkscape gears extension (Aaron Spike, Tavmjong Bah 2007; Juergen Weigert 2014, GPL); boxes/pulley.py is based on droftarts' 'Parametric Pulley with multiple belt profiles' (January 2012, itself based on Prusa Mendel and Thingiverse pulleys) and supplier tooth data. Overlaps with other box generators such as MakerCase and festi.info mirrors (count once), and with Joinery and kyub (HCI research tools for laser-cut joints) [uncertain for MakerCase, not opened]
